Be Used to + Ing Form to Talk About Customs
Be used to is an expression, not a tense. However, it can be employed in the present and past forms. We use it to say we are familiar with or accustomed to something.

Grammatical Structure

 

Be used to is very simple to employ. We simply need to change the tense of the verb “to be” depending on the subject it goes along. In case we need a verb after the expression “used to”, that verb must have the –ing form. Look at the structures:

 

1    Subject + is/are/was/were + used to + verb –ing + complement

 

2    Subject + is/are/was/were/will be + used to + noun + complement

 

Examples:

 

Present

I’m used to checking my PC every day for viruses or any other threat as the first thing I do when I arrive to my office.

 

Past

I preferred my old office. I was used to its big windows that provided lots of natural light. My actual office is much darker.
I'm used to this sort of computer threats all the time, Mrs. West.
In my previous job I was used to the assessment of an Information Technology Security Audit that tested us on how well we were working on security controls.
Data Loss
Data loss is the damaged or destruction of information due to failures in the storage, transmission and processing processes within an information system.

To avoid data loss from happening companies implement robust equipment and security processes and protocols to back up and restore information. Two concepts related to this topic are usually explored. They are:

{"rows":2,"columns":2,"cells":["{\"type\": \"text\", \"content\": \"-\tdata loss and \"}","{\"type\": \"text\", \"content\": \"(permanent loss of information)\"}","{\"type\": \"text\", \"content\": \"-\tdata unavailability \"}","{\"type\": \"text\", \"content\": \"(temporary loss of information)\"}"],"styles":" intro_table_border"}

Companies adopt or design and develop security systems to avoid data losses primarily. Data unavailability may be caused due to a network outage which is a temporary cause. However, it should be included in the risk analysis plan that may affect the system.

Types of Data Loss
  • Caused by intentional action: Intentional file or program deletion
  • Caused by unintentional action: accidental file or program deletion, administration errors, inability to read unknown file format, misplacement of CDs or Memory sticks
  • Caused by failure: power failure, hardware failure, a software crash or freeze. Software viruses or reduced usability, such as not checking a file delete command. Business failure, and data corruption, such as file system corruption or database corruption.
  • Caused by a disaster: earthquake, flood, fire, natural disaster, tornado, etc.
  • Caused by crime: SQL injection, hacking, theft, sabotage, a malicious act, such as a worm, virus, hacker or theft of physical media.

Cost of Data Loss
Data that is needed but unavailable because of data loss is highly expensive. The cost of a data loss incident is directly related to the value of the data and the span of time that it is unavailable. You may think about:
  • The cost of keeping working without the data.
  • The cost of creating the data once again.
  • The cost of informing users in the occurrence of a compromise.

Prevention of Data Loss and Data Unavailability
Companies can take a series of preventive measures to avoid data loss and data unavailability from occurring:
  • Installation of multiple power circuits with battery backup and a generator to be protected against power failures.
  • Installation of an uninterruptable power supply to protect computer's drives against sudden power spikes.
  • Installation of a journaling file system and RAID storage to be protected against software and hardware failure.
  • Ensuring minimal vibration and movement will protect hard disk drives against damaging the internal components.
  • Ensuring regular data backups to help recover more easily after a data loss event.
  • Ensuring security plans and protocols to prevent the system from user errors, natural disasters and criminal events.

General Manager: We're having lots of problems with our information systems and computers nowadays. Data losses, computer viruses, spyware, and a system attack have been very common. I won't wait here inactively to see how our information assurance gets damaged or is put at risk. So, what alternatives do we have?
IT officer: I'm used to this sort of computer threats all the time, Mrs. West. So, based on the collected information and analysis so far, my team's working on implementing a series of measures to avoid the system susceptibility to fail and prevent it from any form of threat. For example, in my previous job I was used to the assessment of an Information Technology Security Audit that tested us on how well we were working on security controls. Hopefully, we'll implement that functionality by the end of this month. In addition, we're working on the implementation of an Information Security Management System which will operate at its full capacity in about three weeks and …

General Manager: Sorry, but I don't understand anything.
IT officer: Oh, excuse me, Mrs. West. What I'm saying is that I'm used to working with and consequently, we're implementing plans and standards to avoid any vulnerabilities and risk for any of the company's information systems and assets. As you probably know, a vulnerability is a flaw or weakness in the design, implementation, operation or management of a system that could be exploited by a hacker's capability to violate the system's security procedures and controls.

General Manager: And when will we see results?
IT officer: A sensibility program will start next Thursday to let you know what things will be modified in the business to avoid vulnerability. That relates to management procedures, hardware, software, personnel, physical environment, communications equipment, and business operations.
